alternatives.root_cause: A feature flag flipped in flagd turned on a failing code path in one of the flag-driven services (ad, cart, product-reviews or recommendation), degrading frontend's page assembly.
alternatives.why_not: Four services read flagd yet none of them alerted, and a flagged failure usually surfaces as errors in that service rather than pure latency at the edge; still a strong second given the empty change log such incidents produce.

alternatives.root_cause: frontend's process or its outbound connection/thread pool saturated, so it could not issue or complete calls and held requests to their deadlines.
alternatives.why_not: frontend alerted later than the edge and only on latency, suggesting it is relaying a wait rather than originating it; a frozen or exhausted frontend would normally also trip its own error-rate alert.

verdict.summary: A shared downstream dependency of frontend—most likely product-catalog—became slow, so frontend requests piled up waiting and frontend-proxy returned timeout errors to the load generator.
verdict.reasoning: The alerting set is strictly the ingress chain (load-generator -> frontend-proxy -> frontend), the classic signature of 'the caller noticed'. frontend alerts only on latency, a minute after the edge alerts on errors: frontend is still answering, just waiting. frontend-proxy's error alert is consistent with gateway timeouts on hung upstream calls. Nothing in the fan-out (ad, cart, checkout, product-catalog, product-reviews, recommendation) alerts on its own, which is what you expect when a backend gets slow but does not itself error. Among frontend's dependencies, product-catalog is the most load-bearing (frontend, checkout and recommendation all call it) and the most common source of latency in this topology, so it is where I would look first.
open_questions: Per-dependency latency and error rates from frontend's client spans: which upstream call consumes the added wall time?
Does product-catalog log anything during the window, or is it silent (freeze/partition) versus logging slow queries (real latency)?
